sections.title: A visual skill solves a communication problem
sections.explanation: An illustration becomes useful when it helps a particular viewer understand or do something.

items.label: Name the message
items.detail: Choose the one idea the viewer needs to understand.

items.label: Choose a form
items.detail: Use a diagram, photograph, chart or layout that suits the idea.

items.label: Build and review
items.detail: Inspect readability, accuracy, rights and cultural context.

items.label: Test the use
items.detail: Check the finished artefact on the intended device or medium.

sections.takeaway: Judge the visual by the brief and audience, not only by how impressive it looks.

sections.section: 1. Why visual skills matter in non-design careers

sections.title: Diffusion: an intuition, not every tool’s architecture
sections.explanation: In a simplified diffusion example, a trained system iteratively refines noise under conditioning. Image tools can also use other generation architectures.

items.label: Training examples
items.detail: The model learns patterns relating visual content to conditioning information.

items.label: Starting noise
items.detail: A random initial representation provides a starting point.

items.label: Guided refinement
items.detail: Repeated model steps steer the representation toward the requested content.

items.label: Decoded image
items.detail: The result still needs inspection for details, text, bias and meaning.

sections.takeaway: A plausible picture is generated content, not evidence that an event, person or product really appeared that way.

sections.section: 2. How an image generator works (the intuition)

sections.title: Generation, design and editing are different jobs
sections.explanation: Choose the type of tool that solves the current bottleneck rather than forcing one generator to do the whole workflow.

items.label: Generate an asset
items.detail: Create a candidate image from a permitted brief.

items.label: Design the message
items.detail: Arrange text, image and information hierarchy in a layout.

items.label: Edit precisely
items.detail: Crop, repair, mask or resize an existing asset with review.

items.label: Export and test
items.detail: Produce the required format and inspect the actual output.

sections.takeaway: Review current capabilities, access conditions and terms before committing to a tool.

sections.title: A visual brief prevents guessing
sections.explanation: A shared brief makes both creation and review more specific. It supplies constraints the generator cannot infer reliably.

items.label: Purpose and audience
items.detail: Name the desired action and intended viewer.

items.label: Format
items.detail: Set dimensions, orientation and viewing context.

items.label: Must-haves
items.detail: List approved text, marks and factual details.

items.label: Style and constraints
items.detail: Describe visual qualities, rights limits and exclusions.

sections.takeaway: Use placeholders for unapproved details instead of letting the image invent them.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. Reading a brief before you prompt

sections.title: A generated asset still has a rights trail
sections.explanation: Tool terms, input rights, likeness permission and the context of use all matter. No diagram can certify ownership or legal clearance.

items.label: Inspect input rights
items.detail: Confirm permission for references, photographs and source material.

items.label: Check use conditions
items.detail: Review the account terms and intended distribution.

items.label: Review depiction
items.detail: Consider likeness, brands, sensitive context and misleading implications.

items.label: Keep a record
items.detail: Store the relevant source, terms and disclosure decision.

sections.takeaway: Check current terms and obtain qualified review for consequential uses; keep records of the permitted workflow.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can a generated picture serve as proof that a real event happened?
checkpoint.answer: No. It is a generated depiction. Use genuine evidence for factual event claims and disclose synthetic content where it could mislead.

m3-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “Image prompt mastery & editing”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Compose the image request from distinct choices
sections.explanation: The prompt slots describe what is depicted and how it is presented. They are controls to test, not guarantees of precise output.

items.label: Subject
items.detail: Name the main subject and action clearly.

items.label: Setting
items.detail: Describe place, time and relevant context.

items.label: Medium
items.detail: Choose visual qualities such as line art or documentary photography.

items.label: Composition
items.detail: Set framing, layout and space needed for text.

items.label: Lighting
items.detail: Describe light and mood without contradicting the scene.

items.label: Constraints
items.detail: State permitted content, palette and exclusions.

sections.takeaway: Inspect the result even when every slot is specified.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Describe visual qualities instead of borrowed identity
sections.explanation: Concrete vocabulary makes a direction easier to reproduce and review than an artist name or vague praise.

items.label: Medium and texture
items.detail: Specify flat vectors, paper texture, line weight or other visible qualities.

items.label: Framing and light
items.detail: Name shot distance, viewpoint and illumination.

items.label: Palette and exclusions
items.detail: Use approved colours and explicit content boundaries.

sections.takeaway: Avoid imitating a living artist’s identity; describe the visual characteristics you need.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Change one visual decision at a time
sections.explanation: A controlled revision shows which instruction affected the result. A fixed base direction helps keep a set coherent.

items.label: Choose a direction
items.detail: Select a candidate against the brief, not random novelty.

items.label: Change one slot
items.detail: Adjust composition, light or palette with a clear intention.

items.label: Compare the result
items.detail: Check both the intended change and unwanted drift.

items.label: Save the base
items.detail: Keep the reusable instruction and its known limitations.

sections.takeaway: Reference images need permission too, and consistency must be checked rather than assumed.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Choose an edit for the actual defect
sections.explanation: Region repair, canvas extension and ordinary layout edits solve different problems.

items.label: Repair a region
items.detail: Use a mask or selection to target a local visual defect.

items.label: Extend the canvas
items.detail: Add surrounding space while reviewing newly generated content.

items.label: Adjust the layout
items.detail: Crop, position and correct colours in an editor.

items.label: Add verified text
items.detail: Use editable typography and proofread every character.

sections.takeaway: After any edit, recheck the whole image for unintended changes.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. Editing: the second half of the skill

sections.title: Representation needs a deliberate review
sections.explanation: A prompt can repeat stereotypes or depict a community inaccurately even when it is technically successful.

items.label: Set the context
items.detail: Describe the intended audience and avoid stereotyped defaults.

items.label: Check permission
items.detail: Review likeness, references, brands and intended use.

items.label: Inspect the depiction
items.detail: Ask whether people, symbols and details are represented accurately.

items.label: Revise or stop
items.detail: Change a misleading or harmful concept rather than only polishing it.

sections.takeaway: Permission, respectful context and truthful claims matter more than a generation tool’s willingness to comply.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: After inpainting a small defect, what else should you inspect?
checkpoint.answer: Review the whole image for drift, changed meaning, factual details, text, rights and representation—not only the selected region.

sections.title: An asset is not the finished design
sections.explanation: Generation supplies material. Layout, typography, export and review turn it into usable communication.

items.label: Brief
items.detail: Fix purpose, reader and approved details.

items.label: Generate assets
items.detail: Create and inspect candidate visuals.

items.label: Lay out and typeset
items.detail: Arrange the message and add verified text in the design layer.

items.label: Export and inspect
items.detail: Check readability, cropping and meaning in the actual format.

sections.takeaway: Keep factual text editable and verify the final export on the target device.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Map a design feature to its job
sections.explanation: Different AI features accelerate parts of a design process. Availability and paid-tier restrictions can change.

items.label: Layout draft
items.detail: Use a tool to suggest a starting arrangement.

items.label: Asset creation or repair
items.detail: Generate, remove or extend selected visual material.

items.label: Text assistance
items.detail: Draft or translate wording, then proofread it.

items.label: Format adaptation
items.detail: Resize and reflow while checking hierarchy and clipping.

sections.takeaway: An equivalent accessible workflow is more important than a particular branded button.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A small brand kit keeps decisions consistent
sections.explanation: A shared kit records choices so a set can look coherent across people and formats.

items.label: Colour tokens
items.detail: Save approved colours and contrast combinations.

items.label: Type system
items.detail: Define readable headings and body text for each script.

items.label: Marks and spacing
items.detail: Record approved logos, clear space and placement rules.

items.label: Voice and imagery
items.detail: Keep a consistent, respectful language and visual direction.

sections.takeaway: Check that fonts support the languages you actually publish.

sections.section: 3. A brand kit in fifteen minutes

sections.title: Build the narrative before the slide deck
sections.explanation: A generated deck is a draft. A presentation still needs a coherent argument, checked evidence and a clear ask.

items.label: Write the story
items.detail: Choose the audience’s question and decision path.

items.label: Outline messages
items.detail: Give each slide one sentence-level point.

items.label: Add evidence
items.detail: Build charts from verified tables and label their sources.

items.label: Rehearse and revise
items.detail: Check timing, readability and the final request.

sections.takeaway: A decorative picture of a chart cannot replace a chart built from actual data.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A truthful infographic starts in a data table
sections.explanation: Data visualisation encodes measured values. Image generation may invent visually plausible but meaningless marks.

items.label: Check the table
items.detail: Verify values, definitions and the period.

items.label: Choose the encoding
items.detail: Match comparison, trend or distribution to a suitable chart.

items.label: Label honestly
items.detail: Show units, scale, source and relevant limitations.

items.label: Inspect the message
items.detail: Check that the design does not exaggerate the evidence.

sections.takeaway: Use a zero baseline for bar lengths, explicit units and a traceable source.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Design fundamentals work together
sections.explanation: Hierarchy tells the reader where to begin; alignment and spacing make the rest easier to follow.

items.label: Hierarchy
items.detail: Make the most important message clearly identifiable.

items.label: Alignment
items.detail: Line up related elements consistently.

items.label: Contrast
items.detail: Keep text and meaningful marks distinguishable.

items.label: Proximity
items.detail: Place related ideas together and separate unrelated ones.

items.label: Restraint
items.detail: Remove detail that competes with the main message.

sections.takeaway: Use labels and sufficient contrast instead of relying on colour or decoration alone.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 6. Five fundamentals that fix most amateur designs

checkpoint.question: Why should an image generator not draw the bars for a factual infographic?
checkpoint.answer: It can invent shapes and values. Build the chart from a checked table, label the units and source, and inspect the final design.

sections.title: A video workflow combines several tool families
sections.explanation: Clip generation, avatar presentation and editing have different purposes and risks.

items.label: Generated clips
items.detail: Create candidate motion material and inspect continuity.

items.label: Avatar presentation
items.detail: Use an approved synthetic presenter with consent and disclosure.

items.label: Editing
items.detail: Arrange shots, narration, captions and sound into a coherent piece.

sections.takeaway: The finished video needs editorial and factual review regardless of how its clips were produced.

sections.section: 1. Three families of AI video tools

sections.title: A storyboard is cheaper than an avoidable reshoot
sections.explanation: The script and shot list decide what the viewer needs to see before generation starts.

items.label: Write for speech
items.detail: State one message and the intended viewer action.

items.label: Make a shot list
items.detail: Pair script moments with the necessary visual evidence.

items.label: Storyboard
items.detail: Sketch composition and continuity before spending credits.

items.label: Confirm format
items.detail: Check orientation, captions and viewing context.

sections.takeaway: Decide the format early and preserve the factual meaning through every shot.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Describe motion, then inspect motion
sections.explanation: A useful motion request distinguishes subject action from camera movement. Simpler shots are easier to review.

items.label: Start from a clear frame
items.detail: Use a permitted still or a tightly scoped scene.

items.label: Specify movement
items.detail: Name the intended subject and camera motion.

items.label: Generate a candidate
items.detail: Keep the action simple enough to evaluate.

items.label: Review over time
items.detail: Check bodies, objects, text, continuity and implied claims.

sections.takeaway: A convincing first frame does not guarantee believable or truthful movement later.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: An avatar needs more than a script
sections.explanation: A synthetic presenter can create a misleading impression of endorsement or identity.

items.label: Confirm authority
items.detail: Check who may be depicted and for which use.

items.label: Approve the words
items.detail: Verify the script and the consented scope.

items.label: Disclose the medium
items.detail: Tell viewers when the presenter is synthetic where relevant.

items.label: Review the output
items.detail: Inspect pronunciation, lip sync and misleading context.

sections.takeaway: Use permitted stock or consented likenesses, disclose synthetic presentation and approve the actual script.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: The edit is where separate assets become meaning
sections.explanation: Changing shot order, captions or sound can alter the claim even when every source clip is acceptable.

items.label: Place narration
items.detail: Use the approved spoken message as a reference.

items.label: Match shots
items.detail: Keep visuals consistent with the actual claim.

items.label: Caption and mix
items.detail: Correct text, preserve intelligibility and use permitted music.

items.label: Export and watch
items.detail: Review the complete piece on the intended device.

sections.takeaway: Proofread captions against the audio and source, including names, dates and regional-language terms.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. Assembling in an editor (the real work)

sections.title: One short video needs one clear promise
sections.explanation: A short format works best when it introduces a specific problem, delivers a useful idea and names the next action.

items.label: Earn attention
items.detail: Introduce the real problem without a misleading claim.

items.label: Deliver the idea
items.detail: Use a small, coherent sequence with readable captions.

items.label: Give an action
items.detail: Name an appropriate next step.

items.label: Test comprehension
items.detail: Ask viewers what they understood, not only whether they liked it.

sections.takeaway: Do not trade accuracy, accessibility or context for a stronger hook.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Does a consented avatar licence permit any words to be put in that person’s mouth?
checkpoint.answer: No. Check the permitted use and approve the actual script and context. Consent to one use is not blanket approval of every statement.

sections.title: Repurpose the idea, not a decontextualised fragment
sections.explanation: One source can support several formats if its meaning and evidence remain intact.

items.label: Core source
items.detail: Keep the full report, interview or recording as the reference.

items.label: Short visual
items.detail: Translate the main idea into a poster, card or carousel.

items.label: Spoken version
items.detail: Retell for listeners and review against the source.

items.label: Written summary
items.detail: Adapt length and structure without inventing detail.

items.label: Distribution
items.detail: Respect the audience, consent and channel requirements.

sections.takeaway: A shorter extract must not turn a qualified statement into an absolute claim.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Consistency is a repeatable check
sections.explanation: A kit and base prompt reduce drift, while a publication checklist catches the errors they cannot prevent.

items.label: Use the kit
items.detail: Apply approved type, colour, marks and voice.

items.label: Adapt the message
items.detail: Fit the audience and format without changing the claim.

items.label: Run the checklist
items.detail: Review text, rights, accessibility and disclosure.

items.label: Record changes
items.detail: Update the shared template when a recurring problem is found.

sections.takeaway: A template is a starting constraint, not permission to skip review.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Accessibility belongs in the brief
sections.explanation: Clear labels, text alternatives and readable layout help people understand the same message in different ways.

items.label: Readable contrast
items.detail: Check meaningful text and graphics against their backgrounds.

items.label: Text alternatives
items.detail: Describe informative visuals in their actual context.

items.label: Captions and transcripts
items.detail: Provide an accurate written equivalent for speech.

items.label: Language and scale
items.detail: Use suitable wording and inspect the intended screen or print size.

sections.takeaway: Do not make colour, sound or animation the only way to receive essential information.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A visual can mislead without a false caption
sections.explanation: Synthetic realism, identity cues and persuasive layout can imply a fact or endorsement that never existed.

items.label: Reality claim
items.detail: Could someone mistake this for evidence of an event?

items.label: Identity and rights
items.detail: Whose likeness, work, brand or cultural symbol appears?

items.label: Commerce
items.detail: Does the image imply an untrue product result or testimonial?

items.label: Community context
items.detail: Would the depicted audience recognise it as accurate and respectful?

sections.takeaway: Review current policy and legal requirements for the actual use; disclosure is not a cure for every harmful depiction.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Four publication questions make a practical gate
sections.explanation: Before publishing, check reality, permission, context and factual claims separately.

items.label: Real or synthetic?
items.detail: Decide whether the depiction needs clearer labelling.

items.label: Whose rights?
items.detail: Confirm the relevant permission and scope.

items.label: Respectful and accurate?
items.detail: Seek an appropriate reviewer for sensitive context.

items.label: Claim supported?
items.detail: Prove, qualify or remove the factual implication.

sections.takeaway: When a necessary answer is unknown, pause publication and resolve it.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can adding “AI-generated” make a fabricated product testimonial acceptable?
checkpoint.answer: No. Disclosure does not make a false commercial claim truthful or supply the required permission.

items.label: Purpose
items.detail: A coherent, accessible campaign that goes from a specific brief and brand kit to reviewed multi-format assets.

items.label: Build an artefact
items.detail: Create the required work for the stated audience and scope.

items.label: Verify and explain

items.label: Process log

items.label: Accessibility and rights

items.label: Reflection

sections.title: Check the boundaries before the build or release

items.label: Evidence and scope

items.label: Permission and rights

items.label: Human control

items.label: Build deliberately

items.label: Craft and consistency

items.label: Process and fluency

items.label: Brief fit and reflection

sections.title: Use the review habits, not a success formula

items.label: Plan the video early

items.label: Proofread before export

sections.title: Separate tool help from your responsibility

items.label: Trace the evidence

checkpoint.question: Can an image generator supply invented bars for the campaign’s data visual?
checkpoint.answer: No. Build a factual chart from a real cited source, verify the values and label units and scale. A plausible chart image is not data.
